"[]"	"[{\"city\":\"Columbia\",\"state\":\"SC\",\"count\":13},{\"city\":\"ARLINGTON\",\"state\":\"VA\",\"count\":7},{\"city\":\"Miami\",\"state\":\"FL\",\"count\":6},{\"city\":\"UPPER\",\"state\":\"\",\"count\":6},{\"city\":\"RANDOLPH\",\"state\":\"MA\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Naples\",\"state\":\"FL\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Houston\",\"state\":\"TX\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Saint\",\"state\":\"\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Columbus\",\"state\":\"OH\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Grand Rapids\",\"state\":\"MI\",\"count\":4}]"	Most people who fail at Airbnb didn't pick a bad city. They picked the wrong property. And today I'm going to show you the five signs — before you sign anything, before you spend a single dollar — that tell you whether a rental property is actually going to make you money on Airbnb.

Here's what nobody tells you about this business. The property is the bet. Everything else — the furniture, the photos, the listing description — that stuff matters. But if the property itself is wrong, none of that saves you. It's like putting a fresh coat of paint on a car with no engine. It looks great in the driveway. It's not going anywhere. And I've watched people learn this lesson the hard way. They get excited. They find a cute apartment. They sign a twelve-month lease. They furnish the whole thing. And two months in, they realize the numbers don't work. They're bleeding money every single month and they're locked in for a year.

I don't want that for you. So let's talk about how to know — really know — if a property is going to print money or drain your bank account. And I'm not giving you theories. I'm giving you the exact signs I look at, backed by real data from Coach Inayah market data that I pull through my free tool every single day. Let's get into it.

Sign number one. What similar places nearby are already making. This is the biggest one. This is the one that matters more than anything else. And this is the one most beginners skip completely. Before you even think about signing a lease, you need to know what other Airbnb hosts in that same neighborhood are bringing in every month. Not what you hope to make. Not what some guru told you on a podcast. What people are actually making right now in that specific area.

Let me give you a real example. Right now, one of the most searched cities in my tool is Columbia, South Carolina. Thirteen searches just recently. People are looking at Columbia because the rent is low and they're hoping the Airbnb money is high enough to make it work. And when you pull the data, here's what you find. A one-bedroom, one-bathroom property in a market like that is pulling in around two thousand and six dollars a month. That's about twenty-four thousand and sixty-nine dollars a year. The average nightly rate — meaning what you'd charge a guest per night — is ninety-eight dollars. And the property is booked about sixty-seven percent of the time.

Now, why do those numbers matter? Because if the rent on that one-bedroom is, say, eight hundred dollars a month, and you're bringing in two thousand, that leaves you twelve hundred dollars before your other costs. That's a deal worth looking at. But if the rent is fifteen hundred? Now your margin is tiny. One slow month wipes you out. See how this works? You need the real numbers from real listings before you ever fall in love with a property. And you can get those numbers in about thirty seconds using Coach Inayah's Turnkey Tool. I built it specifically for this. You type in a city, you see what every listing around you is actually earning. No guessing. No hoping.

Sign number two. The rent-to-money ratio. I'm going to teach you something right now that will save you more money than almost anything else I could tell you. It's a simple math trick. Take the monthly rent on the property. Divide it by the total money coming in from Airbnb each month. That gives you a ratio. A number. And that number tells you almost instantly whether a deal is strong, okay, or garbage.

Here's the rule. If that number is below zero point four — meaning your rent is less than forty percent of what the property brings in — that's a strong deal. That means for every dollar the property earns, less than forty cents goes to rent. You've got sixty cents left for cleaning, supplies, your software, your insurance, and your actual profit. That's breathing room. That's a cushion.
If that number is between zero point four and zero point five-five, you're in caution territory. It might work, but it's tight. One bad month, one slow season, and you're scrambling.
And if that number is above zero point five-five? Walk away. That means more than half of everything the property earns goes straight to the landlord. There's almost nothing left for you.

Let me bring this to life. Say you find a place in Arlington, Virginia. Arlington is another hot market in the tool right now — seven searches recently. Rents in Arlington are not cheap. You might find a one-bedroom for sixteen hundred a month. If that property brings in three thousand a month on Airbnb, your ratio is sixteen hundred divided by three thousand, which is zero point five-three. That's caution territory. It could work, but you better know your costs inside and out. But if you find a similar property where the rent is twelve hundred and the money coming in is still three thousand? Now your ratio is zero point four. That's a green light. Same city. Same type of property. Completely different outcome. That's why you check the numbers first.

I had a student — I won't say her name — but she came to me ready to sign a lease in Miami. Miami is another popular one. Six searches in the tool recently. She found this gorgeous apartment. Modern kitchen. Rooftop pool. She was in love. But when we ran the numbers, her rent was twenty-two hundred a month and the comparable listings in that building were only pulling in about twenty-eight hundred. That's a ratio of zero point seven-eight. I told her straight up — this property is beautiful, and it will lose you money every single month. She was upset at first. But she thanked me three months later when she found a different property with a ratio of zero point three-eight and started actually keeping money in her pocket.

Sign number three. How often it's booked. This one is sneaky because a lot of beginners focus only on the nightly price. They see listings charging a hundred and fifty dollars a night and they think, oh my gosh, if I just get booked twenty nights a month, that's three thousand dollars. And yeah. That math is correct. But here's the question nobody asks. Are properties in that area actually getting booked twenty nights a month? Or are they sitting empty half the time?

That's why you have to look at how often places are booked. In the data world, we call this the occupancy rate, but think of it like this. If your property is available thirty nights in a month, how many of those nights does someone actually book? If the answer is twenty out of thirty, that's about sixty-seven percent. And sixty-seven percent is actually pretty solid. That's roughly what we're seeing in the Coach Inayah market data for a lot of the properties people are analyzing right now. Sixty-seven percent average across the board.

But here's what you want to watch for. If the average in your area is below fifty percent? That means properties are empty more than half the time. And empty nights earn zero dollars. Your rent is still due. Your electric bill doesn't care that nobody booked. So before you sign that lease, look at what similar properties nearby are actually booking. If they're consistently above sixty-five percent, that's a healthy market. If they're between fifty and sixty-five, proceed with caution and make sure your other numbers are really strong. Below fifty? I'd keep looking.

And by the way, this is exactly what the tool shows you. When you run a property through Coach Inayah's Turnkey Tool, it doesn't just show you the money coming in. It shows you how often places are booked, what they charge per night, and how those numbers change throughout the year. Because here's the thing — some markets look amazing in the summer and terrible in the winter. You need to see the full picture.

Sign number four. The rules in your city actually allow it. I know this one sounds obvious. But you would be shocked — shocked — how many people sign a lease, buy furniture, set up their listing, and then find out their city doesn't allow short-term rentals. Or requires a permit that takes six months to get. Or limits you to only renting your primary residence.

Every city has different rules. Some cities love Airbnb hosts. They make it easy. Some cities are cracking down hard. And the rules change all the time. What was fine last year might be illegal this year. This is one of the first things I tell every single student. Before you look at a single property, check the rules. And I made this easy for you. Step one of the Turnkey Tool is literally a regulation checker. You type in your city and it tells you what's allowed, what's not, and what permits you might need. It takes ten seconds. And it could save you from a ten-thousand-dollar mistake.

Here's a quick story. Columbia, South Carolina — the most searched market in the tool right now — has a much friendlier regulatory environment than, say, certain neighborhoods in Miami or parts of New York City. That's one reason people are flocking to it. The barriers to entry are lower. But you still need to check the specific rules for the specific area you're targeting, because even within one city, rules can change block by block. Don't skip this step. I promise you it's not the exciting part of starting your Airbnb business. But it's the part that keeps your Airbnb business from getting shut down.

Sign number five. The property tells a story a guest would pay for. Now, the first four signs were all about numbers and rules. This last one is about something different. It's about the guest experience. And this is where a lot of data-driven people actually miss the mark.

Think about it from the guest's perspective. When someone opens Airbnb and searches for a place to stay, they're scrolling through dozens — sometimes hundreds — of options. What makes them stop? What makes them click? What makes them book? It's the feeling. It's the story the property tells in those first few photos. A property that's near something — a downtown, a stadium, a beach, a hospital, a university — that's a property with a built-in story. A property that has a unique feature — a balcony with a skyline view, a hot tub, a fireplace, a workspace for remote workers — that's a property guests remember.

Before you sign a lease, ask yourself this one question. If I were a traveler, would I choose this place over what's already out there? If the answer is no, or if the answer is maybe, that's not good enough. Because remember, you're not just competing with hotels. You're competing with every other Airbnb host in that neighborhood. And some of those hosts have been at this for years. Your property needs to stand out or it will sit empty.

Now, can you make an average property work with great photos and great pricing? Sometimes. But your life is so much easier when the property itself has something special. A location. A layout. A view. A vibe. Something that makes a guest say, I want to stay there.
So let me bring all five of these together for you.

Sign one — check what similar places nearby are actually making. Real numbers from real listings. Sign two — do the rent-to-money ratio. Keep it below zero point four for a strong deal. Sign three — check how often places are booked. You want sixty-five percent or higher. Sign four — make sure the rules in your city actually allow short-term rentals before you spend a dime. And sign five — make sure the property tells a story a guest would pay for. Something that makes it stand out.

If a property passes all five of these? That's a property worth pursuing. If it fails even two of them? Keep looking. There are thousands of properties out there. You don't need to force a bad deal. You need to find the right one.

And here's the best part. You don't have to do any of this manually. I built a tool that does all of it for you. Go to coachinayahturnkeytool.com right now. Type in any address. The tool checks the rules, shows you what similar places are making, calculates whether the deal is worth it, and gives you a clear verdict — go, caution, or pass. Fifty-five properties have already been analyzed through the platform. People in Columbia, Arlington, Miami, and cities across the country are using it right now to find their first deal. It's completely free. No sign-up required. Go to coachinayahturnkeytool.com, enter an address, and see the real numbers before you risk real money. Stop guessing. Start knowing.
